$comment: R1770 — `$at` is the SURFACE EXTENT this canon was written against, and
the shell's own paint sweep reads it from here rather than declaring a
size of its own. See `analyzer-inspector-spec.json` for what a pin that
named no size cost this tool.
R1761 — THE DASHBOARD SECTION'S PAINTED SURFACES, written down from the
behaviour reference in neutral vocabulary, so the section can be judged
against something other than its own tables.
WHY THIS IS A SECOND DOCUMENT FOR ONE SCREEN, WHICH IS NORMALLY A DEFECT.
`analyzer-board-spec.json` beside it already specifies five surfaces of
this same screen. They are not the same kind of claim, and the difference
is the one R1758 made the report carry: a surface here is read back out of
a PAINTED FRAME, at any moment, by a running application answering a host.
Two of that file's five are not paint at all — a drop contract is a
declaration a surface publishes, and a drop standing is what a router hands
a source mid-gesture — and the other three exist only while a placement is
in flight, which a wire read cannot arrange.
So that document is judged by a DRIVEN sweep, which can perform a gesture
and ask the declaration; this one is judged from the frame. Splitting them
by evidence rather than by screen is what keeps a section's published
verdict honest: a paint-stamped report that quietly answered two of its
surfaces from a declaration would be exactly the defect R1758 repaired one
level up. The two documents name DISJOINT surfaces and a gate asserts it,
because one word with two documents behind it is the defect R1747 spent a
round on.
WHAT IS THE REFERENCE'S AND WHAT IS THIS BUILD'S. The layout bar's four
parts, the panel's heading and hint, the three groups, the entries' order
inside the first two groups, the footer's two counts and the four cards the
board opens with are all the reference's, read off the screen it states.
Two things are not, and both are recorded as remainders below rather than
written in as if they were: this build's hint offers a second way to place
a widget, and its third group is named for a wider set than the reference's
third.
★ THE ENTRY LIST IS THE REFERENCE'S OWN COUNT, NOT ITS OWN LIST. The
reference's palette PAINTS six reserved entries and its footer says NINE
are reserved — the mismatch is in the reference, and the requirement table
on the same page names all nine. This build lists nine, so its panel and
its footer agree; the three the reference's panel omits sit in the group
their requirement belongs to. Stated here rather than left for a reader to
notice, because a pin that silently completed its source would be a pin
nobody could check against the source.
HOW A PART IS TITLED, AND WHY IT DIFFERS PER SURFACE. Where the reference
fixes the WORDS a reader reads — a panel's heading, a group's heading —
the title here is those words, and the judge reads them back out of the
frame. Where a part is a value or a control whose label the screen changes
as it works, the title is this screen's own name for it and what the pin
fixes is the roster and its order. `crate::judge` says which is which per
surface and why.
R1797 — WHAT THE `board` SURFACE DOES NOT PIN, AND ONE DIVERGENCE THAT
LIVES HERE BECAUSE OF IT. This surface pins the cards the board holds and
their titles, in order. It does not pin WHERE each one sits, so the
placement below is not a remainder it can carry — a divergence declared
against a surface that cannot measure it is refused, correctly, as already
paid.
The reference's opening board puts its latency widget at column 0 of the
fifth row, four columns wide and two rows tall, and R1797 put it there
first. The paint census refused it: a row is 174 pixels and the board
starts 16 in, so row 4 begins at 712, while the canvas is 802 tall and the
card is 332 deep. Its header and its three stat tiles were on screen and
its DISTRIBUTION began exactly at the fold — the one thing a distribution
card exists to show was the one thing cut off.
The reference's first release fills this viewport exactly: four cards over
four rows, 712 pixels in 802. A fifth does not fit by placement, only by
reflow. So the three cards of the third row are four columns each instead
of six and six, which keeps every card whole and visible and keeps the
reference's ROW assignment for all three. The alternative is what the
reference's own eight-widget second-release board does — let the reader
scroll — and it is available here; it was not taken because a card that
shows nothing at rest reproduces a distribution card worse than a narrower
one that shows it.

Drag onto the canvas to place

owed.sentence: `hint` is specified as "Drag onto the canvas to place" and reads "Drag onto the canvas, or click to add"
owed.why: The reference offers one way to get a widget onto the board and this build offers two: every placeable row carries a seat that places one without a drag, which the reference draws as well and does not mention here. The line says both, so a reader is not told to drag when a click will do. Recorded rather than reconciled by deleting the second way, which is the direction this project's rule about the reference runs: what the reference has and this build lacks is built, and what this build has beyond it is kept.

owed.sentence: `operate` is specified as "DIAGNOSTICS · RELEASE 2" and reads "DIAGNOSE & OPERATE · RELEASE 1 + 2"
owed.why: The reference's third group holds three diagnostic widgets. This build's third group holds those and two that ACT on the system under study rather than report on it, so a heading saying only diagnostics would misname half of what is under it. The group's membership is the reference's requirement table's; the heading follows the membership. R1843 widened the release half for the reason R1797 widened `visual`'s: promoting the health seat puts one first-release widget under a heading that named only the second, and a heading naming a single release would be false about part of what is under it. The heading is DERIVED from the membership, so this sentence follows the promotion rather than being edited alongside it.

owed.sentence: `visual` is specified as "VISUALIZATION · RELEASE 2" and reads "VISUALIZATION · RELEASE 1 + 2"
owed.why: The reference books its latency widget under the second release and this build now places it, at the reader's decision, so that group holds one first-release widget beside four second-release ones and a heading naming a single release would be false about half of what is under it. The promotion moves this build TOWARDS the behaviour reference rather than away from it: that prototype's own opening board places latency at column 0 of the fifth row, four columns wide and two rows tall, which is where `board` now puts it. What the promotion waited on was the framework — a latency distribution needs a geometric bucket ladder with an unbounded tail and percentile landmarks, and the charting crate had none of the three until R1797 built them.
